description:
We, the crew of The Vitalauts, looked at the stars and realized a terrifying truth: space is stunning, but it has zero pharmacies. Naturally, we stepped in—not with rockets, but with our sharpest tools: code, AI, and a passion for saving lives.

As young innovators , we’re bridging the 20-minute radio gap between deep space and Earth. With HelioMed, we turn space data into an offline medical co-pilot, keeping future Mars crews safe (and proving you don’t need Mission Control to save lives)!
summary: For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we created HelioMed, a first astronaut health monitoring and decision-support platform designed for the challenges of deep-space missions. Imagine an astronaut millions of miles from Earth on a journey to Mars, facing an unexpected health issue with no internet connection and a one-way communication delay of up to approximately 20 minutes to Mission Control (a round-trip delay of up to 40 minutes). Instead of waiting without guidance, they can turn to HelioMed for accessible health information and structured self-assessment. Informed by NASA’s Human Research Program (HRP) and NASA’s Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight, HelioMed transforms complex space-health concepts into an intuitive, interactive experience. Through an interactive 3D anatomical body model, astronauts can log physical discomfort and review NASA-referenced initial response steps. Looking ahead, HelioMed is designed to support future integration with live spacecraft environmental sensors and biometric monitoring hardware
details:
The Vitalauts' Project Solution

HelioMed is an offline-first astronaut health monitoring and decision-support platform built to support crew well-being during long-duration space missions. When crews travel millions of miles toward Mars, radio signals to Earth can take up to approximately 20 minutes each way—making real-time consultations with flight surgeons impossible. HelioMed addresses this challenge by bringing structured health risk assessment directly onboard the spacecraft. Combining daily physical and behavioral check-ins, simulated cabin environmental telemetry, and an interactive 3D anatomical body model, our platform helps astronauts spot health trends early, visualize discomfort zones in 3D, and follow clear, step-by-step initial response guidance during communication blackouts or delays.

How Does Our Solution Work?

Imagine waking up inside a spacecraft halfway to Mars with sharp lower back pain, poor sleep, and stale cabin air. Instead of flipping through dense manuals or waiting up to 40 minutes for a round-trip reply from Mission Control, you open HelioMed.

HelioMed guides crews through a clear, four-part workflow built on deterministic, rule-based logic:

  • Dual-Role Mission Portal (Astronaut vs. Flight Surgeon): Users enter through a mission gateway and choose between two dedicated workspaces:
    • Astronaut Portal: Built for speed and clarity. Crew members log daily check-ins in seconds and immediately view color-coded feedback on their health status.
    • Flight Surgeon (Medical Officer) Portal: Designed for the onboard medical officer. It provides a fleet-wide overview to review crew check-ins, track logged symptoms over time, and spot active anomaly alerts across the team in one click.
  • Interactive 3D Anatomical Body Model: Powered by Three.js, HelioMed renders a rotatable, segmented 3D anatomical model of the human body. Whenever an astronaut logs discomfort in a specific area—such as the chest, lower back, or left knee—that anatomical zone lights up with a glowing red indicator. Clicking the highlighted zone opens a Guidance Card displaying potential warning signs and NASA-referenced initial response steps.
  • Holistic Physical & Behavioral Tracking: Monitors sleep duration and quality, targeted body discomfort zones, nutrition intake, exercise routines, mass changes in microgravity, psychological stress, crew dynamics, and daily recovery habits (such as hydration and screen fatigue).

Development Roadmap: Current Prototype vs. Future Integration To maintain strict engineering transparency, HelioMed is structured across three clear stages:

  1. Current Prototype: Functional offline-first web application supporting daily health check-ins, interactive 3D anatomical discomfort mapping, rule-based symptom analysis, and plain-language guidance cards.
  2. Simulation & Testing Mode: Uses simulated cabin telemetry (CO₂, pressure, and radiation spikes) to demonstrate and validate how environmental changes correlate with crew symptoms.
  3. Future Spacecraft Integration: Designed to connect directly with real onboard life-support sensors and wearable crew biometric monitors for live local processing.

How Is Our Project Creative & What Factors Did Our Team Consider?

Most health tracking tools resemble intimidating hospital spreadsheets—the last thing a fatigued astronaut wants to navigate during an urgent situation. We took a human-centered design approach by building HelioMed as an intuitive, visual mission dashboard where color-coded 3D anatomy and plain-English guidance cards replace dense jargon.

While designing HelioMed, our team (The Vitalauts) accounted for four real-world spaceflight constraints:

  • Cognitive Load Under Stress: Sleep-deprived or unwell astronauts can struggle with heavy text, so we prioritized visual 3D body mapping and universal status colors (green for normal, amber for caution, red for immediate review).
  • Non-Specialist Usability: Not every crew member is a physician, so every alert outlines clear, step-by-step initial response actions any astronaut can follow.
  • Environment-to-Body Connection: Based on spaceflight research, closed-cabin stressors—altered gravity, radiation, and air quality—directly influence physical and behavioral well-being.

Our Goal & Intended Impact

Our goal is to demonstrate that crew safety and informed health action should never depend on an instant connection to Earth.

  • In Space: Supports future Mars transit crews and deep-space explorers in monitoring physical and behavioral trends and responding promptly to potential warning signs during communication delays.
  • On Earth: The exact same constraints—extreme isolation, unreliable internet, and limited access to specialists—affect remote communities worldwide. HelioMed’s offline-first interface can be adapted for rural clinics, offshore stations, research outposts, and disaster-relief zones when communications are down


Tools and Technologies Used

Platforms & Deployment:

  • Google AI Studio → for prototyping, prompting, and building the core AI workflow.
  • Vercel → for hosting and deploying the web application.
  • GitHub → for source code management and version control.

AI Models:

  • Gemini → for powering the intelligent chat, symptom analysis, and triage workflows.

Data Sources & Content:

  • NASA Human Research Program (5 Hazards) → for integrating deep-space physiological risks directly into triage protocols.
  • Canadian Space Agency (CSA) Cansat / Radiation Telemetry → for neutron radiation monitoring
  • Offline 3D Anatomical Datasets → for powering the interactive body map to pinpoint pain zones

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

We used Google AI Studio and Gemini as supportive resources throughout the project. Specifically:

  • Design & Prototyping: Used Google AI Studio and Gemini to brainstorm user-flow ideas, test prompt logic, and build offline-first emergency navigation workflows.
  • Implementation Guidance: Prompted the AI for coding suggestions regarding frontend integration, offline data handling, and best practices.
  • Debugging Assistance: Used AI to help identify, explain, and resolve frontend rendering and data-sync errors during development.
